m.t: When God Knocks at the Door
o: Beloved Father, I begin this day by thanking you, because you never grow tired of seeking me. Many times I have turned my back on you, and yet you kept knocking patiently at the door of my heart. Today I want to open to you again, without reserve, so that you may govern my thoughts, my words, and my decisions.

Lord Jesus, you said that you stand at the door and knock, and that if anyone hears your voice and opens, you will come in and eat with him. Help me recognize your voice amid the noise of the morning. Teach me that my life no longer belongs to me, that I have been crucified with you, and that it is now you who live in me. Take from me the pride that wants to do everything its own way, and give me a simple and obedient heart. Give me the humility to admit my mistakes and the courage to begin again as many times as it takes, leaning on your grace.

I pray for those who doubt, for those who are searching for answers, and for those who do not yet know you. Use me today to speak of you with kindness, through my actions more than through speeches. May every encounter of the day be an opportunity to show your love. Keep me from evil and lead me in your peace. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 29, 1898, Clive Staples Lewis, known around the world as C. S. Lewis, was born in Belfast, Ireland. When he was nine years old, his mother died of cancer, a loss that marked his childhood. In time he drifted away from the faith and declared himself an atheist through his teenage years and young adulthood.

Lewis became a professor at Oxford University and a scholar of literature. Yet his heart remained restless. He himself told how in 1929 he gave in and admitted that God was God, knelt and prayed, perhaps, in his own words, the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England. Some biographers place this moment in 1930, but all agree it was a gradual surrender, not a sudden impulse.

The step toward faith in Jesus Christ came in 1931, after a long late-night conversation with his friends J. R. R. Tolkien and Hugo Dyson as they walked along Addison's Walk in Oxford. From then on, he put his intellect and his pen at the service of the Gospel.

Over the years, Lewis became known for his clear way of explaining the faith. He said that he believed in Christianity as he believed that the sun had risen, not only because he could see it, but because by it he could see everything else. Many readers have found in his writings an invitation to think honestly and to open their hearts to Christ.

During World War II, he gave radio talks on the BBC about the Christian faith, between 1941 and 1943, which were later collected in the book “Mere Christianity.” Between 1949 and 1954 he also wrote the seven books of The Chronicles of Narnia, in which many readers find a reflection of Christ's love. C. S. Lewis died in 1963, but his books continue to help people around the world think with clarity and believe with the heart.
m.c: May the voice of Christ go with you today in every decision and every encounter. Walk with the assurance that God knows you, seeks you, and sustains you. Go out with joy, for his grace is sufficient for everything this day will bring.
m: The story of C. S. Lewis reminds us of something beautiful: God knows how to wait. For years Lewis resisted, argued, and looked for explanations, and the Lord kept knocking patiently at his door. He does the same with each one of us. Jesus said that he stands at the door and knocks; he does not break it down, but waits for us to open it willingly.

Perhaps today you see yourself on both sides of this story. Perhaps you have honest questions about faith and think God takes offense at them. But the Bible shows us that God is not afraid of our questions; what he wants is for us not to close the door. Or perhaps you opened it to him long ago, but lately you have left the door only ajar, busying yourself with your own affairs more than with his voice.

Paul described the heart of the Christian life in these words: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. This means that today we do not have to sustain our lives by our own strength. We can ask Christ to live through us at work, at home, and in our relationships with others.

For today, I offer you something practical. Before you begin your tasks, set aside two minutes of silence to say: Lord, come in and govern this day. And during the day, when someone speaks harshly to you or you are tempted to give up, remember that this door remains open. If someone is looking for answers, listen to them with patience and respect, just as God did with you.

t.s: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
o: Lord God, as night falls, I thank you for this day. Thank you for every blessing, big or small, and also for the trials that taught me to depend on you more. You have been my refuge when I felt tired and my light when I did not know which way to go.

Like Paul and Silas, I want to learn to praise you even in the dark nights. You are not far away when I feel shut in by worry, by illness, or by circumstances I cannot change. You know how to break chains and open doors in your time. Today I hand over to you everything that holds me back: fear, resentment, guilt, and anxiety. Set me free from these, Lord, and fill my heart with your peace. Thank you for your Word, which comforts me when I have no words left, and for your Spirit, who prays for me when my strength fails.

Thank you, because salvation comes by believing in the Lord Jesus Christ. Bless my home, my loved ones, and those who needed me today. Grant me restful sleep and a hope-filled awakening. May my last thought today be a song of gratitude to you. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On his second missionary journey, Paul and Silas arrived in Philippi, a city of Macedonia. There Paul freed a young slave girl from a spirit that controlled her. Her owners, seeing that they had lost their source of profit, dragged Paul and Silas before the authorities and accused them of disturbing the city.

The crowd rose up against them. The magistrates ordered that their clothes be torn off and that they be beaten with rods. After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely. He put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in stocks.

Anyone would expect complaints and tears. But the Bible says that at midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; at once all the doors flew open and everyone's chains came loose.

That same night, the jailer brought Paul and Silas into his home, washed their wounds, and set a meal before them. It is beautiful to see that the very man who had locked them up was now caring for them. The Gospel turned fear into hospitality and harshness into tenderness.

The jailer woke up, saw the doors open, and, thinking the prisoners had escaped, was about to take his own life. But Paul cried out to him not to harm himself, for they were all there. Trembling, the jailer fell down before Paul and Silas and asked what he must do to be saved. They answered him: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household. That very night, the jailer and his whole family were baptized, and he rejoiced with his entire household that he had come to believe in God.
t.c: May your heart sing with gratitude tonight, even if the day has been long. God keeps working in the darkness and takes care of you and your household. Rest peacefully, knowing that his peace guards your mind until dawn.
m: The most surprising thing in this story is not the earthquake, but what Paul and Silas did before it. They were wounded, their backs bruised and their feet in stocks, and yet they sang. Their praise did not immediately change their circumstances, but it changed their hearts and bore witness to those who were listening.

As you end this day, perhaps it has not been easy. Perhaps you are carrying a pain or a burden that feels like a chain. This story does not ask you to pretend that everything is fine. It invites you to do what they did: pray and praise God even in the midst of weariness, believing that he is present and that he listens.

Notice also that others were listening to them. When we give thanks in the midst of difficulty, our peace reaches those around us. Your family, your coworkers, or your neighbors may learn more from your serenity than from many words. And notice the jailer: that night began in fear and ended with a house full of joy.

Tonight, before you sleep, try something simple. Sing or hum a song of praise you know, or whisper: thank you, Lord, for this day. Hand over to God every chain you feel and rest. He can act at midnight, when you least expect it, and his peace is greater than any wall. Do not underestimate the value of your quiet witness, either. Someone may be watching how you respond to hardship, and your calm trust may open a door for them toward God.
